prompt.context_jp: 面倒見のよさで知られる芝崎の目には、いつになく張り切った光____宿っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 面倒見のよさで知られる芝崎の目には、いつになく張り切った光____宿っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits — a new, noticeable element appearing in Shibazaki's eyes.

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is introducing something newly noticed — an unusual sparkle in Shibazaki's eyes. New, perceptible information takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark 光 as already-known topic, which clashes with 'いつになく' (unusually). を doesn't fit an intransitive 宿る.

contrast_examples.en: Tears welled up in his eyes. (new appearance → が)
That light is special. (already-known topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 逃げるように自分の席へ戻ると、待ち構えていたの____相馬健のからかい混じりの視線だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 待ち構えていたの____相馬健のからかい混じりの視線だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. This is an identificational 'what-was-waiting-was-X' structure.

feedback.correct_en: 'The thing that was waiting' is the topic/known slot; the new info (Souma's teasing gaze) comes after the copula. 〜のは〜だ is a cleft focus pattern using は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 'what was waiting' the new info, breaking the cleft focus. を doesn't fit a nominalized subject.

contrast_examples.en: What I want is time. (cleft → は)

prompt.context_jp: 芝崎さん 面倒見____いいからなぁ
prompt.prompt_jp: 芝崎さん 面倒見____いいからなぁ
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Souma is pointing out a specific trait of Shibazaki.

feedback.correct_en: When describing which specific attribute someone has (〜が いい/多い/上手だ), が picks out the particular trait. 芝崎さん is topic; 面倒見 is the characterizing attribute marked by が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は after 面倒見 would make it a second topic and sound disjointed. に doesn't fit an adjectival predicate like いい here.

contrast_examples.en: As for height, he's tall but… (contrast → は)

prompt.context_jp: ここ 友田さん____お店なの
prompt.prompt_jp: ここ 友田さん____お店なの
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'This is Tomoda-san's shop' — a revealing identification.

feedback.correct_en: Here の links two nouns possessively — 'Tomoda-san's shop'. The sentence identifies this place as belonging to him.
feedback.incorrect_en: は or が after 友田さん would make him a topic/subject predicating something else, which doesn't produce 'Tomoda's shop'.

contrast_examples.jp: 友田さんがオーナーだ。

prompt.context_jp: 僕____ ただ たくさんの人に おいしいステーキを食べてほしい
prompt.prompt_jp: 僕____ ただ たくさんの人に おいしいステーキを食べてほしい
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Tomoda is stating his own personal stance/dream.

feedback.correct_en: Tomoda is setting himself as the topic to declare his own position ('As for me, I just want…'). This topic-comment structure takes は.
feedback.incorrect_en: 僕が here would sound like exhaustive listing — 'I (and no one else) want…' — too assertive for his modest confession.

contrast_examples.en: I'll do it (not anyone else). (exhaustive → が)

prompt.context_jp: 舞____ 私と同じ東京第一銀行に 勤めてるんですよ
prompt.prompt_jp: 舞____ 私と同じ東京第一銀行に 勤めてるんですよ
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Ayana is giving information about Mai as the known topic.

feedback.correct_en: Ayana just said she works at Tokyo Daiichi, so 'Mai too (works there)' uses も to add Mai to the same category.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would just topicalize Mai neutrally and miss the 'same as me' nuance (私と同じ). が would introduce Mai as new subject, odd when she's already present.

contrast_examples.en: Mai is also a banker. (addition → も)
Mai is a banker. (plain topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 相馬さん____ 今や ウチの いちばんのお得意さまなんだよ
prompt.prompt_jp: 相馬さん____ 今や ウチの いちばんのお得意さまなんだよ
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The father is identifying Souma as the top customer.

feedback.correct_en: Souma is the known topic (Mai just mentioned him), and the father comments on his status. Topic-comment → は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would exhaustively identify Souma as 'the one who is the best customer,' sounding like a reveal rather than an explanation to Mai.

contrast_examples.jp: 相馬さんはお得意さまだ。
contrast_examples.en: Souma is a regular customer. (topic → は)

contrast_examples.jp: いちばんのお得意さまが相馬さんだ。
contrast_examples.en: The top customer is Souma. (identificational が)

prompt.context_jp: 娘の口ぶりを聞きつけて、幸三の手____一瞬止まった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 娘の口ぶりを聞きつけて、幸三の手____一瞬止まった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for a sudden observable event.

feedback.correct_en: A sudden, observed event — Kozo's hand stopping — is new information presented to the reader. New-event descriptions take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would topicalize 幸三の手 as if contrasting it with something else, which doesn't match this narrative beat.

prompt.context_jp: 店の名を聞いた瞬間、舞の頬にじんわりと熱____上がった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 舞の頬にじんわりと熱____上がった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for a sensation appearing on Mai's cheeks.

feedback.correct_en: 熱 is a new sensation appearing — a classic 'new element on the scene' use of が for an intransitive event.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark 熱 as a known topic, which clashes with the sudden onset. を doesn't fit intransitive 上がる.

contrast_examples.en: Her face turned red. (new event → が)
The fever (we were watching) went down. (known topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: ところが背後から声をかけてきたの____思いがけない相手だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 背後から声をかけてきたの____思いがけない相手だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. This is a cleft structure revealing who called out.

feedback.correct_en: 〜のは〜だった cleft: 'The one who called out was an unexpected person.' The nominalized clause is topic (は), and the new info (unexpected person) comes after.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 'the one who called out' the new element, undoing the cleft focus structure that makes 思いがけない相手 the punchline.

contrast_examples.en: The one who came was him. (cleft → は)

prompt.context_jp: 品川支店の誰か____東京ダラスという会社から 賄賂を受け取ったみたいなんです
prompt.prompt_jp: 品川支店の誰か____東京ダラスという会社から 賄賂を受け取ったみたいなんです
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Otsuka is revealing new, unidentified information.

feedback.correct_en: 誰か is an indefinite 'someone' — brand new information. Indefinite subjects and newly introduced referents take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: 誰かは is grammatically odd; は presupposes a known topic, but 誰か is specifically unknown.

prompt.context_jp: 支店長・八木の視線____、初対面から刺すように鋭かった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 支店長・八木の視線____、初対面から刺すように鋭かった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. The narrator is characterizing Yagi's gaze.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence introduces Yagi and then characterizes him via his gaze — a topic-comment pattern. は sets 八木の視線 as topic and comments on it.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present the gaze as new/exhaustive info — fine in a sudden observation, but here the preceding clause has already set him up, making は more natural.

prompt.context_jp: ウチの融資に____一点の曇りもない！
prompt.prompt_jp: ウチの融資に____一点の曇りもない！
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Yagi is emphatically denying any problem with his loans — contrastive emphasis.

feedback.correct_en: には is a contrastive/emphatic topic marker — 'as for our loans (unlike others), not a single blemish.' The 〜には〜もない pattern emphasizes the denial.
feedback.incorrect_en: にが is ungrammatical here, and を doesn't fit this existential/attributive construction.

contrast_examples.en: Here (in contrast), there's no problem. (contrast は)
There's a problem there. (new info が)

prompt.context_jp: 融資案件を決める力を 持っているの____ なにも支店長だけじゃない
prompt.prompt_jp: 融資案件を決める力を 持っているの____ なにも支店長だけじゃない
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle. Souma is correcting Mai's assumption with a cleft.

feedback.correct_en: 〜のは〜じゃない is a cleft that frames the known clause (who has the power) as topic and corrects the predicate. は fits the cleft focus.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 'the one who has the power' the new element, but here Souma is correcting Mai's existing assumption, not introducing a new subject.

contrast_examples.en: The one at fault isn't me. (cleft → は)
I'm the one at fault. (identificational が)

prompt.context_jp: 舞は嫌な予感を覚えつつ、示された頁に視線____落とした。
prompt.prompt_jp: 示された頁に視線____落とした。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that marks what she lowered.

feedback.correct_en: 落とす is transitive, and 視線 is the direct object being lowered onto the page. を marks that object.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 視線 the subject (as if the gaze fell by itself). に would duplicate the destination marker already on 頁に.

prompt.context_jp: 友田さんは よく こういうお店 ____んですか？
prompt.prompt_jp: 友田さんは よく こういうお店 ____んですか？
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb form that fits Mai's polite question to Tomoda.

feedback.correct_en: 来られる is the honorific form of 来る, elevating Tomoda whom Mai has just met. Polite deferential tone fits a getting-to-know-you conversation.
feedback.incorrect_en: Plain 来る would be too casual for someone she just met. 来てる is also plain progressive and lacks respect.

contrast_examples.jp: よくいらっしゃるんですか？

prompt.context_jp: 芝崎の熱心な仲人ぶりに、舞はいい加減____てきた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 舞はいい加減____てきた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the expression for 'getting fed up'.

feedback.correct_en: うんざり captures being fed up/sick of something persistent — fitting Shibazaki's relentless matchmaking. いい加減 collocates naturally with うんざり.
feedback.incorrect_en: がっかり means 'disappointed' (unmet expectation), not weariness. びっくり is 'surprised,' which doesn't match the ongoing annoyance.

contrast_examples.jp: 長い説教にうんざりした。
contrast_examples.en: I got fed up with the long lecture.
I was disappointed by the result.

prompt.context_jp: 一度 家に帰られて 着替えてから お____になったらいかがでしょう
prompt.prompt_jp: 一度 家に帰られて 着替えてから お____になったらいかがでしょう
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the keigo verb stem for 'go out'.

feedback.correct_en: お出かけになる is the standard honorific form of 出かける (to go out). Souma is being mock-polite to Mai about her 'date.'
feedback.incorrect_en: お行きになる is awkward (the standard honorific of 行く is いらっしゃる). お帰りになる means 'to go home,' which contradicts the context.

contrast_examples.jp: お出かけになりますか？

contrast_examples.en: Will you be going? (honorific of 行く)

prompt.context_jp: 素っ気なくもなく、____もいない礼のメールを打つのは、思いのほか難しい。
prompt.prompt_jp: 素っ気なくもなく、____もいない礼のメールを打つのは、思いのほか難しい。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word that pairs with 素っ気ない to describe the tonal balance Mai wants.

feedback.correct_en: 浮かれる means 'to get giddy/overly excited.' Mai wants a tone that is neither cold (素っ気ない) nor over-eager (浮かれた) — this contrast is the natural one.
feedback.incorrect_en: 怒る (angry) and 疲れる (tired) don't contrast meaningfully with 素っ気ない in a thank-you email about a date.

contrast_examples.jp: デートで浮かれている。

prompt.context_jp: 30になると 男性からの誘いが ____と落ちる
prompt.prompt_jp: 30になると 男性からの誘いが ____と落ちる
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the mimetic adverb for a sharp, sudden drop.

feedback.correct_en: ガクッ(と) is the mimetic for a sudden, steep drop — fitting the alarming survey claim that invitations plummet after 30.
feedback.incorrect_en: そっと ('gently') and ゆっくり ('slowly') contradict the dramatic, sensational tone of the magazine.

contrast_examples.jp: 売上がガクッと落ちた。

prompt.context_jp: ____ お客さまの前で
prompt.prompt_jp: ____ お客さまの前で
prompt.prompt_en: Choose Tomoda's apology to his guests after scolding staff in front of them.

feedback.correct_en: すみません is the polite apology Tomoda uses to his customers, matching the formal register of the whole dinner conversation.
feedback.incorrect_en: ごめんね is too casual for a restaurant owner addressing guests. どうも alone is a vague greeting, not an apology.

prompt.context_jp: どうか ____ ウチの店を救ってください！
prompt.prompt_jp: どうか ____ ウチの店を救ってください！
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the phrase for a desperate, formal plea.

feedback.correct_en: どうか お願いします is a set phrase for an earnest formal appeal. Otsuka is pleading with a bank employee he just met.
feedback.incorrect_en: 頼むよ is far too casual for begging a stranger. どうぞ means 'please, go ahead' and doesn't fit a plea for help.

contrast_examples.en: Come on, help me out. (casual plea)

prompt.context_jp: どこに こんな____が 残ってたのかってくらいの！
prompt.prompt_jp: どこに こんな____が 残ってたのかってくらいの！
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the slang noun Ayana uses for an unexpectedly great catch.

feedback.correct_en: 掘り出し物 literally 'dug-out item' = a hidden gem/unexpected find. Ayana uses it jokingly to describe the handsome Tomoda.
feedback.incorrect_en: 落とし物 means 'lost item' and 忘れ物 means 'something forgotten' — neither has the 'rare find' nuance.

prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds more natural coming from Ayana to her close friend Mai about tonight's dinner?

choices.text: 女同士で気兼ねなく ガッツリ おいしい物 食べようって 楽しみだね
女性のみなさまで ご遠慮なさらずに たくさん おいしい物を 召し上がりましょう

feedback.correct_en: Between close friends planning a casual dinner, slangy words like ガッツリ and 気兼ねなく with a plain 〜ようって fit the register perfectly.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B uses honorific 召し上がる and 〜なさらずに, which sounds like a hotel concierge speaking — wildly over-polite between friends.

contrast_examples.en: Let's eat a ton! (casual peer talk)

contrast_examples.jp: たくさん召し上がってください。

prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural as a restaurant owner's quick instruction to a staff member?

choices.text: ビスクを ロブスターに変えて クラブも足せばいいんじゃないか？
ビスクをロブスターに変更させていただき、クラブも追加なさってはいかがでしょうか？

feedback.correct_en: A boss giving quick operational instructions to a subordinate uses direct, casual-polite language like 〜ばいいんじゃないか. It's efficient and fits the kitchen's pace.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B's layered keigo (〜させていただき, 〜なさって, 〜いかがでしょうか) is customer-facing register — bizarrely over-polite from boss to employee.

contrast_examples.jp: こうすればいいんじゃないか？
contrast_examples.en: How about doing it this way? (boss to staff)

contrast_examples.jp: こうなさってはいかがでしょうか。
contrast_examples.en: Might you do it this way? (to a customer)

prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural as a rinten inspector explaining their visit to a branch manager?

choices.text: 過去の融資資料に いくつかの不備が 見つかりましたので そのチェックと指導にまいりました
過去の融資資料にいくつか不備があったから、チェックと指導に来たよ

feedback.correct_en: Addressing a branch manager, humble まいりました and 〜ましたので maintain the professional distance expected in inter-branch communication.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B uses plain 〜から and 来たよ — far too casual when meeting another bank's leadership for the first time.

contrast_examples.jp: ご指導にまいりました。
contrast_examples.en: I've come to offer guidance. (humble, formal)
I came to coach you. (casual peer talk)

prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural for Tomoda hinting at a flirty 'we're connected' moment?

choices.text: 僕たち 縁があるみたいですね
僕たち 関係があるみたいですね

feedback.correct_en: 縁がある suggests a fateful/pleasant connection — perfect for a soft romantic hint. It's warm and tasteful.
feedback.incorrect_en: 関係がある literally means 'to have a relationship/connection' but often implies something transactional or even scandalous — jarring in this flirtation.

prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural when Otsuka describes his boss's kindness to someone he just met?

choices.text: 学歴も経験もなかった僕を 雇ってくれたんです
学歴も経験もない僕を 雇ってやったんです

feedback.correct_en: 〜てくれた shows gratitude from Otsuka's perspective — Tomoda did him the favor. This correctly expresses the emotional direction.
feedback.incorrect_en: 〜てやった means 'did (them) a favor' from the giver's standpoint — if Otsuka says this, he's bizarrely claiming he hired himself as a favor. Direction is wrong.

contrast_examples.en: The president hired me (and I'm grateful).
I hired my junior as a favor to him.
